title: SSA says no local field office permanently closed since January 2025
description_short: SSA said it had not permanently closed or announced closing any local field office since Jan. 1, 2025, while noting one announced hearing-office closure in White Plains.
description_medium: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration said it had not permanently closed or announced closing any local field office since Jan. 1. The agency said it had announced one hearing-office closure in White Plains, New York. It also said many spaces submitted to GSA for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms without assigned employees.
description_long: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration said it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office since Jan. 1 of that year. The agency separately said it had announced one hearing-office closure in White Plains, New York. SSA said it works with congressional delegations before permanent closures and reassigns employees from affected offices to other locations. It also said many spaces submitted to the General Services Administration for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms without assigned employees, as most hearings were held virtually. The agency said temporary local-office closures can occur because of weather, damage or facilities problems, followed by reopening. The statement distinguishes local field offices from a hearing office and small hearing rooms. It does not establish that DOGE closed ten local offices or that the White Plains decision resulted from DOGE.

original_record.title: DOGE Closed Social Security Offices, Left Disabled Facing 135-Mile Trips
original_record.synopsis: By February 2025, DOGE began closing at least 10 Social Security field offices, including the White Plains, NY hearing office serving seven counties with 2,000 pending cases. Closure would force elderly and disabled beneficiaries to travel up to 135 miles to the next office, potentially into another state. SSA staffing was already at a 50-year low when DOGE arrived, and ProPublica reported many closures targeted low-income, disabled, and orphaned recipients with no internet access.

children_proposals.title: Rescissions Act cancels future Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations
children_proposals.description_short: The Rescissions Act of 2025 rescinded Corporation for Public Broadcasting appropriations for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, effective upon enactment on July 24, 2025.
children_proposals.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025. Section 2 made the act’s rescissions effective upon enactment and rescinded Corporation for Public Broadcasting amounts made available for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. The statute establishes those appropriations rescissions; it does not state a $1.1 billion total or quantify station-level losses.
children_proposals.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025, following a June 3 presidential rescission request. The enacted statute says the rescissions took effect upon enactment. Section 2(b)(20) identifies and rescinds amounts made available to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, including amounts provided through the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025. This was a statutory cancellation of specified future CPB appropriations. The law does not state that $1.1 billion was cut and does not quantify effects on individual public television or radio stations. Those amounts and downstream effects require separate appropriations records or station-level evidence. The text identifies the fiscal-year appropriations it rescinded and makes that rescission effective upon enactment; it does not itself report station receipts, local programming changes or individual broadcaster losses.

The page named news organizations and highlighted stories that the administration characterized as misleading, biased or otherwise objectionable. The event is the publication of a government webpage identifying media organizations and disputing coverage. Its labels should remain attributed to the White House rather than repeated as factual judgments. The tracker’s launch does not establish a count of anti-media social posts, federal investigations of broadcasters or settlements by media companies. Those are separate claims involving different dates, actors and evidence. The reporting supports the page’s launch and its attributed content, while broader claims about coercion require separate evidence. These characterizations are the administration’s labels, not independent findings.

original_record.title: Trump's All-Out War on the Press: $32M in Forced Settlements, 215 Attack Posts, and a Media Offenders Blacklist
original_record.synopsis: Trump's second term saw his long-running enemy of the people rhetoric against journalism convert into systematic, government-backed suppression of the free press at a scale unprecedented in American history. The Freedom of the Press Foundation documented 215 anti-media posts by Trump on Truth Social in 2025, and Poynter's Press Freedom Watch recorded 76 distinct federal actions against journalists during the year. Media companies were coerced into paying $32 million in settlements: ABC paid $15 million toward Trump's presidential library to drop a defamation suit over George Stephanopoulos's on-air statement that Trump was found liable for sexual abuse, and Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump's lawsuit over 60 Minutes editing — with critics noting Paramount was simultaneously seeking government approval for a Skydance merger, creating an explicit coercion dynamic. On November 28, 2025, the White House launched a media bias tracker on its official website naming and shaming outlets as misleading, biased, exposed, listing the Boston Globe, CBS News, and the Independent as media offenders of the week. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr opened eight investigations into NPR, PBS, ABC, NBC, and CBS; Congress voted in July 2025 to cancel $1.1 billion in subsidies for NPR and PBS. Independent journalist Mario Guevara, who had a valid U.S. work permit, was arrested while covering immigration protests in Atlanta, held for 110 days in conditions he described as including 22-hour daily solitary confinement, then deported to El Salvador — a country he had fled due to death threats — despite his charges being dropped.

title: Three Ivanka Trump marks receive provisional Chinese approval
description_short: Three Ivanka Trump marks received provisional Chinese approval on April 6, 2017; 16 was the total registered portfolio.
description_medium: An Associated Press report published April 18, 2017, said China provisionally approved three of Ivanka Trump’s company’s marks on April 6 for jewelry, bags and spa services. The report said the company had 16 registered Chinese trademarks overall and 32 applications pending. It also placed the approvals on the day of the Mar-a-Lago dinner attended by Ivanka Trump, Jared Kushner and President Xi Jinping, without establishing that the timing reflected influence.
description_long: An Associated Press report published April 18, 2017, said Ivanka Trump’s company received provisional approval from China on April 6 for three trademarks covering jewelry, bags and spa services. That evening, Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner attended a Mar-a-Lago dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife. The report distinguished the three approvals announced for that date from the wider trademark portfolio: it said the company then had 16 registered trademarks in China and 32 pending applications, and that four marks had received preliminary approval since the inauguration. The report also discussed the family’s stated ethics safeguards and concerns raised by former government ethics officials about business and policy overlap. This proposal records the specifically reported approval and dinner chronology. The timing alone does not establish that the dinner influenced the trademark decisions, and the 16 registered marks should not be presented as 16 approvals issued on April 6.

The report said there were 16 registered marks overall and 32 pending applications.

original_record.title: Ivanka Trump Receives 16 Chinese Trademarks Approved During Xi Negotiations
original_record.synopsis: On April 6, 2017, the Chinese government approved 16 trademarks for Ivanka Trump's brand in categories ranging from jewelry to spas, while her father Donald Trump simultaneously hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at Mar-a-Lago for diplomatic negotiations. The approvals came after years of pending applications and materialized almost precisely as the summit was underway. Ethics watchdogs immediately flagged the timing as a blatant conflict of interest, noting that Ivanka served as a de facto White House adviser with no official title. The episode illustrated how the Trump family's commercial interests were intertwined with U.S. foreign policy in ways that blurred the constitutional emoluments clause.

original_record.title: Trump Pursues Retaliatory Investigation of Former CIA Director Gina Haspel

Haspel had previously refused Trump's requests to classify and suppress intelligence assessments and had been involved in decisions about the Ukraine whistleblower complaint. Legal observers noted that targeting former intelligence officials for authorized disclosures or for declining to participate in illegal activities represented a profound chilling effect on the entire intelligence community. Former CIA officials described the investigation as an attempt to criminalize professional independence.

original_record.title: Trump Claims 'Absolute Immunity' for Any Presidential Action
original_record.synopsis: Trump and his legal team formally asserted in April 2025 that the Supreme Court's July 2024 immunity ruling in Trump v. United States granted him absolute immunity from accountability for essentially any action taken in office, including actions clearly outside core executive functions. The expansive interpretation went far beyond what even the conservative Supreme Court majority had written, claiming that virtually any presidential act could be characterized as official and thus immune from criminal or civil accountability. Constitutional scholars described the claim as incompatible with the rule of law and the principle that no person is above the law. The claim was being tested in multiple ongoing criminal and civil proceedings against Trump.

original_record.title: Trump Misspells 'Hereby' as 'Hearby' in Nuclear Weapons Tweet
original_record.synopsis: In an official presidential tweet regarding nuclear weapons policy, Trump misspelled 'hereby' as 'hearby,' creating an error in a post that was meant to carry the weight of presidential authority on one of the world's most sensitive security issues. The tweet was part of Trump's attempts to assert control over nuclear policy via Twitter, bypassing traditional diplomatic channels. Critics noted the irony of a president who claimed superior intelligence making elementary spelling errors on consequential policy statements. The misspelling added to a long catalog of similar errors in Trump's tweets, raising questions about basic proofreading and communication standards at the highest levels of government.

original_record.title: Trump Pardons Joe Arpaio a Second Time
original_record.synopsis: Among Trump's Day One pardons in January 2025, Trump included a second pardon for former Arizona Sheriff Joe Arpaio — the same individual he had already pardoned in 2017 for criminal contempt of court related to racial profiling. The redundant pardon was widely mocked as an act of performative loyalty-rewarding with no legal necessity, since Arpaio had no new federal convictions requiring clemency. Legal commentators noted it was a signal to Trump's base that he viewed the pardon power as a political reward mechanism, not a constitutional tool for justice or rehabilitation. The double pardon of the same individual for the same conduct had no precedent in American presidential history.

original_record.title: Trump Claims He 'Saved the Economy' with Tariffs Despite Every Major Economist Disagreeing
original_record.synopsis: Throughout May 2025, Trump publicly claimed that his tariff policy had 'saved' the American economy despite near-universal condemnation from mainstream economists, business leaders, and international institutions. The IMF, World Bank, and major economic research organizations all projected the tariffs would reduce US GDP and raise consumer prices. Trump selectively cited cherry-picked data while ignoring the broader picture of market turmoil and credit downgrades. The disconnect between Trump's claims and economic reality exemplified his administration's relationship with facts.

original_record.title: Trump Ends All Federal LGBTQ+ Health Programs on Day One
original_record.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed executive orders that effectively ended all federal LGBTQ+-specific health programs, including the HHS Office of Minority Health programs addressing health disparities among LGBTQ+ individuals, CDC programs tracking HIV among gay and bisexual men, mental health crisis resources specifically targeting LGBTQ+ youth at elevated suicide risk, and federally funded community health center programs serving LGBTQ+ patients. The orders directed federal agencies to cease collecting demographic data on sexual orientation and gender identity, making it impossible to track health disparities. The Trevor Project and other LGBTQ+ mental health organizations reported immediate spikes in crisis calls from LGBTQ+ youth following the executive orders, citing fear and distress over the removal of federal recognition.

original_record.title: Trump Proposes Constitutional Amendment Removing Judicial Review of Executive Actions
original_record.synopsis: In April 2025, senior Trump White House officials floated and Trump publicly endorsed a proposal for a constitutional amendment that would strip federal courts of the power of judicial review over executive branch actions — effectively overturning Marbury v. Madison, the foundational 1803 Supreme Court decision establishing the principle that courts may strike down government actions that violate the Constitution. The proposal would have required a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of states to become law, making its passage highly unlikely. Nevertheless, the public endorsement of eliminating judicial review by a sitting president was treated by constitutional scholars as an unprecedented statement of intent to fundamentally alter the American constitutional order. Legal historians noted that no prior president had openly proposed dismantling the constitutional check that most fundamentally distinguishes a constitutional republic from an autocracy.

original_record.title: Trump Eliminates Independent Court Oversight of Immigration Detention
original_record.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration rescinded Biden-era settlement agreements and federal monitoring programs that had placed independent court oversight over conditions in immigration detention facilities — oversight mechanisms established after documented abuses including deaths in custody, inadequate medical care, and use of solitary confinement. The removal of oversight mechanisms meant that the administration could operate immigration detention facilities without independent verification of conditions, compliance with minimum standards, or accountability for mistreatment. Civil rights organizations immediately reported a spike in reported abuses at detention facilities. Federal judges who had supervised settlement agreements were told the executive branch was withdrawing from the agreements unilaterally. Legal scholars noted that courts retain inherent authority to enforce their own orders and that the administration's claim it could simply withdraw from court-approved consent decrees without judicial approval was legally incorrect.

original_record.title: Trump Ends All Federal Family Planning Programs
original_record.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration terminated all federal Title X family planning grants — the only dedicated federal program funding contraceptive services, STI testing, and reproductive health counseling for low-income individuals — and eliminated all other federal family planning program funding. Title X had served approximately 4 million patients annually at clinics across all 50 states, providing services including birth control, cancer screenings, and STI treatment. Over 1,600 health centers that depended on Title X funding were forced to reduce services or close. The termination disproportionately affected low-income women, women of color, rural residents, and people without health insurance. Public health researchers projected that the elimination of family planning funding would lead to an increase in unintended pregnancies, maternal mortality, and unsafe abortions.

original_record.title: Trump Ends Equal Access to Justice Act Funding
original_record.synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration moved to end enforcement and funding of the Equal Access to Justice Act — the federal statute that allowed private citizens and small businesses who prevailed in lawsuits against the federal government to recover attorney's fees, providing a critical deterrent against government overreach and an incentive for individuals to challenge unlawful government actions in court. The administration's DOJ began systematically opposing EAJA fee awards in cases where the government had lost, even in cases where courts found the government's legal positions were not substantially justified. Combined with defunding of legal aid organizations and rollbacks of agency enforcement, the effective gutting of EAJA made it dramatically harder for ordinary Americans to challenge unlawful government actions that harmed them.

original_record.title: Trump Charged GOP Fundraising Committees Above-Market Rates at His Properties
original_record.synopsis: Throughout his presidency, Trump's political operation charged Republican National Committee and other GOP fundraising committees above-market rates for events held at Trump properties, directing donor money into the president's personal business. Data compiled by campaign finance watchdogs showed the Trump campaign and related political committees paying Trump Organization entities tens of millions of dollars for venues, catering, and services at rates that independent analyses suggested exceeded comparable commercial offerings. The financial flows created a system where Republican small-dollar donors were effectively subsidizing the Trump family business. Congressional Democrats argued this arrangement made Trump personally dependent on maintaining his political position to sustain business revenues—creating a structural conflict of interest between Trump's private financial interests and his exercise of presidential duties.

title: White House officials used Signal to discuss Yemen operations
description_short: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal to discuss military operations in Yemen in a group chat that included a journalist.
description_medium: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal in a group chat to discuss planned military operations in Yemen. The chat accidentally included journalist Jeffrey Goldberg, who later reported on the messages. Reuters reported that officials said steps had been taken to prevent a recurrence. The reporting documents a specific Signal-use incident, not a government-wide ban on encrypted messaging.
description_long: In March 2025, senior Trump administration officials used Signal to discuss planned U.S. military operations in Yemen in a group chat that accidentally included a journalist. Reuters reported that the thread described an imminent bombing campaign against Houthi militants in Yemen. Jeffrey Goldberg of The Atlantic was added to the private chat alongside Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Goldberg disclosed the messages publicly on March 24. On March 31, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the White House considered the case closed and that steps had been taken to prevent recurrence. Reuters also reported that House Intelligence Committee Democrats requested an independent inquiry and leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee asked the Pentagon to investigate the leak. The reporting concerns this specific Signal thread; it does not establish a government-wide ban on Signal, WhatsApp or other encrypted messaging apps.

facts: Senior administration officials used Signal for a group discussion about Yemen operations.
Journalist Jeffrey Goldberg was included and disclosed the messages March 24.
Officials described later steps and congressional requests for inquiries.
The article does not support a government-wide messaging-app ban.

unsupported_claims: The Trump administration banned Signal, WhatsApp or similar encrypted apps for all federal employees
The chat was created to enable government surveillance of employees

original_record.title: Trump bans encrypted messaging apps for federal employees over spying concerns
original_record.synopsis: The Trump administration banned federal employees from using encrypted messaging applications, effectively requiring communications to remain accessible to government surveillance and monitoring. The ban targeted apps like Signal, WhatsApp, and others that provide end-to-end encryption, forcing government employees to use less secure communication channels. Cybersecurity experts warned the ban actually made government communications more vulnerable to foreign intelligence services, while the administration's real motivation appeared to be monitoring internal dissent among federal workers.

title: OCC gives World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval for a bank charter
description_short: OCC gives World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval for a bank charter
description_medium: On August 17, 2026, CNN reported that the OCC gave World Liberty Trust Company preliminary conditional approval to pursue a national trust-bank charter. Further requirements remained before it could open. The coverage raised conflict concerns because the Trump family has a financial interest in World Liberty Financial; it did not report a finding of regulatory misconduct.
description_long: In August 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency gave World Liberty Trust Company preliminary conditional approval to pursue a national trust-bank charter, according to CNN’s report republished by KTVZ. The approval was not a final charter and did not authorize the firm to operate as a bank. The reporting says additional requirements remained, including a final review before the company could open. CNN identified World Liberty Trust as a trust-bank applicant connected to World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s cryptocurrency venture. The coverage reported that the Trump family has a financial interest in World Liberty Financial and described concerns about Trump-appointed banking regulators overseeing a family-linked company. Those are conflict concerns raised by critics, not a finding that officials acted improperly. The event is a conditional regulatory step; the company’s final charter and actual operations were unresolved in the reports.

title: OCC conditionally approves World Liberty Trust bank application
description_short: OCC conditionally approves World Liberty Trust bank application
description_medium: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported conditional OCC approval of World Liberty Financial’s application for World Liberty Trust Company, a national trust bank. The article said further requirements remained before it could open and argued the Trump family’s stake raised conflict concerns. Its legal and ethical framing is commentary; the approval did not establish misconduct or permit the bank to operate.
description_long: On August 18, 2026, The New Republic reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency had granted preliminary conditional approval to World Liberty Financial’s application for a national trust bank called World Liberty Trust Company. The article stated that the Trump family owned 38 percent of World Liberty Financial and received 75 percent of the company’s cryptocurrency revenue. The OCC approval was not permission to open: the applicant still had to raise capital, satisfy other conditions and complete pre-opening review. The New Republic says the Trump family holds a substantial ownership stake in World Liberty Financial and receives revenue from its cryptocurrency business. It argues that the approval raises a conflict because the family could benefit from a company receiving federal banking approval under an administration led by Trump. Those ownership details and the conflict argument are claims reported in the article, not a finding of misconduct. The event is the regulator’s preliminary approval; the article’s corruption characterization is opinion. The charter process remained incomplete in the report.

title: OCC grants World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval
description_short: OCC grants World Liberty Trust conditional preliminary approval
description_medium: The OCC granted World Liberty Trust Company preliminary conditional approval to pursue a national trust bank charter. The company still had to satisfy capital, governance and pre-opening requirements before it could conduct business; the letter did not authorize it to operate as a bank. Reporting raised conflict concerns but identified no finding of misconduct.
description_long: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued preliminary conditional approval for World Liberty Trust Company to pursue a national trust bank charter in August 2026. The OCC letter states that this step is not final approval and that the company may not begin banking business until it meets specified conditions and receives the agency’s final approval. Requirements include raising capital, establishing compliance and information-security policies, obtaining other regulatory approvals and requesting a pre-opening examination. If capital is not raised within 12 months or the bank does not open within 18 months, the preliminary approval expires. HuffPost reported the approval as a development involving World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company associated with the Trump family. The reports raised conflict-of-interest concerns because of that family connection, but the OCC letter does not find misconduct or say the company was already operating. The event is a conditional licensing step; whether the applicant will satisfy the requirements and receive a final charter remained unresolved.
